en: Homage to Mīnanātha!

Make that very space from the center of space within yourself; place space in the middle of the self. With the mind fixed externally in the void, the nose-tip is clearly said to be the point of steady restraint.
Fashion correctly the reality as it truly is, as spoken by Lūyipāda, within the fold of the *barhis* grass.
Thus it was said:
"Above is empty, below is empty, and the center is empty and free from affliction."
Then Līlāpā spoke of emptiness—emptiness... emptiness—as the reality itself, as taught by the Buddha.
This truth was spoken by the Buddha:
by gazing at the tip of the nose, the *brahmagranthi* is dissolved.
Through the cessation of the breath, all is emptiness within the womb;
and by the grace of Macchendra, the lotus of emptiness shall manifest.
When the resonance of the sound of the syllable Oṃ causes the mind to withdraw [from] the wind,
one should assign the deities to the limbs, as proclaimed by Virūpā and Lūyi.
The body,
consisting of nine apertures, leaks like the holes of a jar.
Therefore, having realized the state of Brahman through the cessation of the ninefold path, [one attains liberation].
Therefore,
both the stainless body and the embodied soul are free from defilement;
through the grace of Virūpākṣa, they realize the state beyond becoming.
Established in the nature of emptiness, situated between the two paths,
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and all others dissolve into that place; everything dissolves there.
These [practices], together with their secret portions, arise from the application of the Lūyipā-krama.
The Lūyī-krama is free from both sin and merit, and devoid of upward-moving vital breath (*ūrdhvodhva-vāyu*).
When the mind and breath are motionless, having made the self inconceivable through contemplation,
this reality shines forth by the grace of the Lord of Lūyi.
Reality shines forth like space; the embodied self is always perceived as being like space.
But the Lord Jālanīpa, who is empty of both the external and the internal, is the lotus.
It is empty, devoid of all conceptual constructions, pure awareness, undecaying and immortal.
Pure.
The consciousness, tranquil and immovable from the very beginning, shines forth as the self-pervading like space;
through the grace of Lūyī, Bhusuku is liberated.
Having abandoned the three states, the yogin attains that fourth state; and having reached that state, he enters the world as the All-pervasive One, like a spider moving through its web.
Having made the heart-lotus the hearth, the withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) is the inner fire-drill (*araṇi*).
One should correctly perceive the fire of the *ciyā* through the friction of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), just as [fire is produced from] Telīśa and Lūyipākrama.
The six sense faculties divide even emptiness into pieces;
the collection of the six sense faculties dissolves like a bird caught in a net falling into a well.
By means of the restraint of the breath,
the inhalation (pūraka) consists of the six sense faculties; by the restraint of the nine apertures, he is the playful child, the Sugata.
The playful sword that severs [ignorance],
whose self is the body of its Lord, supremely pure, unborn, unmanifest, and eternal.
Pure, manifest,
alone, and stainless, the pervasive one is Kukkurīpāda, the son of Lūyīpāda.
Within the space at the gateway of Brahman, the mind merges into the wind; therefore,
as spoken by Lord Kṛṣṇa and Indra, the Lord Kṛṣṇa is all-pervading like the ether.
When the bindu is uttered,
all dissolves into its own place through the binding of the semen and breath.
And the Candrabandha [is performed] with the ḍheṅkī through the sequential yoga.
When the wind flows while remaining in the center of the clearly opened tip of the nose— [the left] nostril— ?
That mind dissolves into its own offspring; this is the *dhvaṃkahṇī* method of Saraha.
Thus it has been said: "This mind is the delusive Māyā, consisting of the error of dualistic conceptualization;
having cast it aside, one should meditate upon Brahman as non-dual, both with and without parts."
Thus it shines forth partless, O Nīlī, according to the teaching of the Sugata.
Just as products such as molasses and sugar are derived from juice, so too is sugarcane;
likewise, O Caṇḍavīra, the ultimate reality appears through the excellence of its playful manifestation.
Just as the one sun shines in all reservoirs of water,
so does that Kadārika; they call him Lūyipāda, and he who is the Krama is Kadārika.
The third deity speaks; you two do not know that reality.
The reality (*tattva*) that is to be known as supreme, which alone remains here in this very reality— this is what is proclaimed [as *Indrabhūta*].
That reality is all-pervading, without support, as spoken by Kamalāmbara.
Just as in the case of consciousness ending with the vital breath (*prāṇa*),
these specific states of the self existing in the realm of conventional usage would likewise end with the aggregate of its own kind.
Having correctly understood the reality of Māhilavīra’s state,
he [attained] that reality through his own effort.
The moon withdraws the elements through the gem-like nature of the joys and sorrows of birth.
Untouched by sufferings, all-pervading, and of the nature of consciousness, I am stainless;
through grace, they proclaim me as the moon-source and the means for the removal of darkness.
Therefore, the wise man who is devoid of the notion of a self has no fear from anything whatsoever,
even upon attaining that which is called yoga— the formless ultimate reality.
Kṛṣṇavīra speaks by the grace of Sarvabhakṣa;
Kṛṣṇavīra [gloss: a fisherman or boatman] is merged in the three, in the single-thorned well, in the six, and within the intervals between the moon and the sun.
In Ekaṇṭhakūpa,
the great yogin Vīraghaṭha was exhorted by Viruvānā.
Situated in the midst of upward and downward breath, abiding in the transcendent void;
resembling ten million suns, yet formless and incomparable.
Among them, the dwelling-places of thought were [constructed] by Jālanīdāsaka with his knees.
Smell, taste, form, touch, sound, and likewise the mind—
wherever these have gone, do not make them return from that place.
Bound solely by his own breath, he is pure, like a young bird in a net.
Pure,
sixteen finger-breadths in height, it is situated above the moon and sun;
sixteen finger-breadths above.
But that, having become equalized and remaining forever in the form of space,
dissolves into its own place along with the breath and the mind for the wise one.
This sequence of the Bhāṭṭa school is stated by Virūpākṣa as well.
When the knowledge of the *bhiṇḍu* has been realized, when the knots of the granthi have been severed, and when the multitudes of doubts regarding the auspicious and inauspicious have been exhausted,
and the seed of worldly existence has been burnt away, one should abide in the Supreme Self. Then, the Hero of Light shines forth, liberated from birth, through the grace of Kaṇha.

Joined with the joy of union (*jānapī*), having made the five sense-objects the companions of thought, and having rendered the mind supportless, it dissolves into the pair of drops (*bindu*) called the reality of bliss (*ānanda-tattva*).
Kahṇudāsa says that smoke has been transmitted through a lineage of those who have realized the further shore.
The mental power (manaśakti) certainly attains immobility in the place of the jar;
it is known as the power of the bell (ghaṇṭhaśakti), which leads to the state of Rudreśa.
When one personally hears the resonance of the sound *ghaṃ* within that [space],
then reality shines forth through the yoga of the sequence of the limbs of the body.
Devoid of the science of grammar and devoid of the circle of the letter *jo*,
with knowledge situated in the *brahmagranthi*, the mind is said to be the flight-path of Indra; that which is called *duducandra* is declared to be the lotus and the light.
The supreme and the abstinent,
the restraint of the upward and downward breaths;
the moon and sun, the *ālikāli*, and the seed-syllable free from death, as well as the mindful breath.
The moon and sun, the vowels and consonants—this is the essence of the two parts; and that sequence is the manifestation of non-becoming.
One's own nature, when unmoving and free from discursive thought, proceeds in a state of uninterrupted continuity;
having become perfectly absorbed in the station of light, it is considered to be utterly tranquil.
Knowledge arises from that quality; it is known as the noose of Kaṅkaṇapāśi.
The mind is to be understood as entering [into objects]; this has been declared by Buddhi-kāma. This has been declared by Buddhi-kāma.
Knowledge alone is the threefold form declared by Śiva as one;
it consists of Kodālī, Lūyipāśin, and [the third].
The yogin should purify the six measures of body, speech, action, and mind, along with the six neutral [elements]. Being completely purified and stainless in nature, he attains the stage of Saraha.
That which is eternally free from old age and death, whose nature is beginningless,
yet resides within the body— this very thing is most manifest in the world as gnosis, the non-dual flavor of mind, the innate clarity.
Knowledge always produces [itself] within one's own body;
thus say the inhabitants of Dvāravatī regarding the grace of Virūpākṣa.

When the senses are conquered and the mind is always subdued, one must conquer the palate; practice the contraction of the tongue. Therefore, with diligent effort, bring the mind to a state of immovability.
They proclaim the reality of Gavāru through the grace of Gorakha.
The jar, which is the garment of the lotus (the sky), dissolves into space; the mind dissolves into space. *līyate* \ms; *mana*. [8v]
In that regard, one should perform the *svāsasa* rite using *koṃkila*, *cora*, *gaṅgī*, and *pāśī*.
The body is always seen as empty space; the self is motionless, stainless, all-pervading, and untainted. The reality shines forth clearly, like the sound of a string set in motion.
The reality [of the state] beyond the mind is the very expanse of space itself, its body pervading everything without exception.
Space has sound as its quality, and sound is called Brahman. The Supreme Self, abiding in the state of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), is Mahīdharadeva and Lūyipāśiśa.
He who knows that which is called Brahman— as it is manifested when all diversity has been shaken off and dispersed—
becomes one with that unsurpassed, supreme bliss. He becomes absorbed in that.
The subtle deity speaks thus with serene confidence regarding the destruction of Virūpā.

Just as space exists both inside and outside of jars, so too does Brahman abide within all physical bodies; yet, when one perceives the "I" in the body as a limited self, that cognition leads to the bondage of saṃsāra.
This is for the sake of binding [the breath],
as spoken by Gorakṣa through the grace of Macchendra.
The nose, tongue, body, form, sound, and mind are also supreme;
through these six, the gnosis of equal flavor— the great elixir of the nectar of immortality— dissolves into the locations of space.
Coraṅgī is the disciple of Lūyipā.

Abandon existence and non-existence, O you who abide in the equal flavor of intrinsic nature! Free from the three positions, the all-pervading supreme state is declared to be "eating everything" through the grace of Lūyipāda.
Like the sky, with the wind as its characteristic, and as immovable as the earth;
like the sun and fire, O wise one, in that which is called beginningless and endless.
While awake or in deep sleep, whether wandering or standing still, whatever occurs—those who know reality call that the state of liberation; I am the servant of that Kaṇhu.
Having thus understood the nature of Prakṛti and Puruṣa, one who has transcended the endless web of conceptualization and attained the supreme state becomes a Kevalin, delighting in the Self alone.
He who, through grace, has attained this very *sakhapila*— the method of *bhusuku*—
which is incomparable in all states of existence, beyond the reach of words of non-duality, and free from attachment; [he is like] the potter.
When Brahman has been apprehended by the intellect, the Self becomes all-pervading, like the sky of its own birth.
O wise one of jewel-like intellect, you have spoken of the restraint of the senses;
O self-controlled one, the winds that have entered the junctions of the channels are dissolved at the location of the *ghaṇṭhā*.
By its very nature, having attained the state of formlessness within its own body,
it is called *sāntipā*, the reality [attained] through the grace of Macchendra.
That gnosis which is free from the three types of gnosis is indeed gnosis itself;
through the thorough knowledge of that very self, it becomes the state of the knowable by itself.
When the state has been spoken by Caṭa with joyful favor,
it is beyond conceptual construction, eternally established in the expanse of space.
"Completely liberated from all entities, remaining as immovable as the earth—
this is the view of Nāgārjuna, spoken by the Ḍākinī herself."
Free from disease, free from appearance, formless, and undisturbed;
liberated from all attachments, this state of innate self-awareness shines forth, proclaimed by the voice of the Sage.
Glossed thus: "Taking hold of the mind that is like the ocean, the [mental] states dissolve of their own accord.
Free from both self and other, it is knowledge alone, devoid of a self."
Furthermore, he speaks of the essence, the auspicious clarity of the feet;
[it is] the sky-pervading space, to be contemplated within one's own body.
Bearing a body though bodiless, they contemplate the supreme goal.
When this has been spoken, one should contemplate this lotus-stalk within the throat;
having stood in the midst of the void, one should effect the dissolution of the crooked and the straight lines into the signless and incomparable.
This is the doctrine of Vīra-stambha, which he himself proclaimed;
having perceived his own breath alone, he emerged through the tip of the nose.
The five senses are dissolved and the mind remains free from attachment;
one who possesses such wisdom shines like the lotus in the sky.
One should contemplate abiding in the interval by means of the cessation of the two paths;
and one should direct the mind toward that interval, O wise one, as proclaimed by the venerable Bhartṛhari.
The mind is not fixed in space, neither in the subtle nor the vast;
it is not in existence, nor in non-existence, nor even in its own movement.
I do not know that reality which cannot be seen even by one who dwells within it;
by the grace of the Teacher, I worship Markaṭī, who is like a monkey.
The mind is the ocean on one hand, and the mind is likewise the moon;
therefore, this full moon is established within one's own heart on the new-moon day.
By the grace of Sogaḍa, Goṇḍa is conjoined with the void (śūnya);
above it are the digits of the moon and fire, and below it is the digit of the sun under control.
One who has conquered the senses should practice in the station situated in the sky.
This was spoken by Pehākara through the grace of Gorakha.
The instruction regarding the reality of self-awareness is the word of the Guru;
by means of the "new well" analogy, make the mind as vast as the sky.
The body is for the purification of the self; it is the pleasing of Māhila.
Knowledge resides in the mind and the body, as well as in the wind and space.
Having become equal in flavor with the four elements, one should cause it to enter at the end of the body;
this has been explained by means of the analogy of oil residing within a vessel.
They drink the nectar of the stream and do not even release their breath;
the wise man, having bound the mind at Oḍiyāna, should place it in the void.
By the grace of Gorakha, Oḍiyāna is revealed;
the mind, free from sense objects, remains established in the midst of sense objects.
Those who desire the *piṇḍa* are said to be established in both the immovable and the movable;
they proclaim the true nature of reality (*tattvasadbhāva*), as spoken by the Nāgas and the cowherds.
Since this karma existed prior to the arising of knowledge, it becomes like a seed placed in a fire, consumed by the crest-flame of knowledge.
The qualities of the stainless one shine forth like the words of Kaṅkana;
above the crescent moon is fire, and above that, the sun is situated.
In the midst of that fire and sun, there is the space named Rati;
in that space, the mind comes to rest—this is the "Heroic Mind" (vīracitta) as taught by Gopāla.
[... Desire, anger, greed, delusion, and envy—
pride, egoism, and impurity— one should abandon these among them.
Equal toward a slave and a friend, equal toward an enemy, and likewise toward pain and pleasure;
alone, free from desire, peaceful, ungreedy, with senses conquered;
enduring cold and heat, and regarding a clod of earth and gold as the same.
Such is this supreme knowledge of the unmanifested conduct.
Thus ends the *Jñānamālā*, which illuminates the true nature of reality as realized by the Siddha Anādi-Śrī-Lūyīpāda and his lineage, beginning with Corāsī.
This treatise has been written for the sake of sentient beings, by means of reasoning that accords with the truth, and for the purpose of bringing about the welfare of all sentient beings.
